title: Long Reading Comprehension Passages
tagline: Year 4 — Passages of 180–250 words: following an argument across paragraphs, with detail, inference, tone, purpose and vocabulary questions

introduction.overview: Long passages test stamina and structure-spotting. The authors argue, qualify and conclude, and the questions are built on those moves. The method is to read once for structure (claim, support, turn, conclusion), mark the turn words (but, yet, however, even then), and answer each question from the relevant lines rather than from memory. Wrong options typically exaggerate, reverse or add to what the passage says.
introduction.placementRelevance: Long RC sets with 5–7 questions are the standard verbal item in advanced company tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Reading long reports and extracting the argument is a daily professional skill.

learningObjectives: Find the claim, support and turn in a long passage
Answer detail questions from the text

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A turn word (but, yet, however, even then) signals the author's real point or a qualification.

coreDefinitions: Claim: the main assertion of the passage.
Turn: a point where the argument qualifies or reverses.
Purpose: why the author wrote the passage (explain, argue, warn).
Exaggeration: an option stronger than the text.
Reversal: an option that states the opposite.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A long passage is a short argument with illustrations. Find the argument, and the illustrations explain themselves.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Mark the first-sentence claim, the turn word and the last sentence. Those three usually carry the answers to main-idea and purpose questions.

mainNarrative: In the passage on maps the claim is that maps are selections made for purposes. The support is the history (power) and the examples (road atlas, geological map). The turn is "Even then the idea was never fully realised". The conclusion is the advice to ask who made the picture and why.
A detail question such as "When did the idea of a neutral map arise?" is answered by one line: when printing made maps cheap and surveying made them accurate.
An inference: digital maps make hidden choices, because software decides which names appear at which scale. The passage does not say digital maps are worse.
In the attention passage the turn is "The result is an uneven bargain". The author is analytical, not hostile to technology, and ends with an open question.
In the buildings passage, the claim is that survival depends on use as well as construction. The final sentence restates it: a building is saved by people who find a reason to use it.

deepDiveAspects.title: Last sentences
deepDiveAspects.content: In argumentative passages the last sentence often restates the main point in memorable form.

deepDiveAspects.title: Open endings
deepDiveAspects.content: An author who ends with an open question has not taken a firm side on it.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Mark claim, turn and closing sentence in one reading and go back to lines for details.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a true but irrelevant option

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Options with always, never or only are usually wrong.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: The passage rarely asks you to agree, only to follow.

easy.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

For most of history, a map was an instrument of power as much as of navigation. Rulers commissioned maps to record the land they claimed, and the decisions about what to show were political. A river might be drawn larger than life because it marked a border; a rival's town might be left blank. Only when printing made maps cheap and surveying made them accurate did the idea arise that a map should simply describe the world. Even then the idea was never fully realised. Every map is a selection: a road atlas ignores the height of hills, a geological map ignores the roads, and a tourist map enlarges the museums. The cartographer's real skill lies not in showing everything but in deciding what to leave out. Modern digital maps seem to have solved the problem by letting the user zoom, but the same choices are made invisibly by software that decides which names appear at which scale. The lesson for any reader of maps is the same as it was for the courtiers of old: ask who made this picture, and for what purpose.

The passage is mainly about
options: how every map is a selection made for a purpose
easy.correctAnswer: how every map is a selection made for a purpose
easy.explanation: The passage moves from political maps to selective modern maps and ends by advising readers to ask who made a map and why.

placementStyle.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Economists once assumed that information was always valuable: the more people knew, the better their decisions. The spread of cheap digital media has complicated this view. When messages arrive faster than anyone can read them, the scarce resource is no longer information but the attention needed to process it. Platforms compete for that attention with notifications, autoplay and endless feeds, and what they measure is time spent, which is easy to count, rather than benefit gained, which is not. The result is an uneven bargain. Users pay with attention and receive free services, yet the value of a minute of attention varies enormously: a minute spent learning a skill and a minute spent scrolling look the same on a usage chart. Some designers now argue for products that help users finish tasks and leave, measuring success by problems solved instead of hours held. Whether such products can survive against rivals that maximise engagement is an open question; much depends on whether users learn to value their own attention as highly as advertisers do.

The phrase "uneven bargain" implies that
options: users receive more than they give
what users give and what they receive are not balanced
placementStyle.correctAnswer: what users give and what they receive are not balanced
placementStyle.explanation: Users pay with attention and receive free services whose value varies, so the exchange is not balanced.

placementStyle.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Visitors to historic towns often assume that old buildings survive because they were better built than modern ones. The truth is more selective. In any century most buildings are poorly made, and most of them vanish within a few generations. What survives is the small fraction that were well made, but also the fraction that remained useful. A sturdy warehouse that became a market, a church that kept its congregation and a palace that became a museum were all altered and repaired by people who needed them. A magnificent building with no purpose, by contrast, tends to decay however well it was built. Durability therefore comes from two sources: the strength of the structure and the willingness of later generations to keep paying for its upkeep. Conservationists who focus only on the first miss the second. A building is saved less by its stones than by the people who find a reason to use it.

The passage mainly argues that preserving old buildings requires
options: continued use as well as strong construction
placementStyle.correctAnswer: continued use as well as strong construction
placementStyle.explanation: The last sentence says a building is saved less by its stones than by those who find a reason to use it.
